title: Cross-modal representation learning, with applications to search in radiology reports and auto-filling of report templates
summary:
It has now been sufficiently demonstrated that algorithms with artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning (DL) methods in radiology, show very good diagnostic performance in some areas, comparable to that of a radiologist. The training of these AI systems is now based on what is known as supervised training; here a large number (thousands for each pathology) of images are presented to the neural network together with the desired outcome (desired K-System output). For this purpose, all images used for training must be annotated by experienced radiologists, i.e. abnormalities in the image which the class should recognize must be marked by radiologists for training. This method is very laborious and, since the annotation has to be carried out by experts, expensive. Thus, the availability of annotated data sets represents the main bottleneck for the development of new AI systems for radiology. In this study, based on the latest AI basic research, methods are to be developed that will enable these extensive and expensive annotations of the image material to be largely dispensed with in the future to be able to The basic idea is to use a combination of image and findings for the training, i.e. several modalities.
In summary, methods are to be developed that will enable the creation of AI algorithms in the future with significantly less effort and smaller amounts of data than is currently the case.
conditions: Diseases for which radiological images are created.

interventions.name: Retrospective inclusion of all patients who received radiological imaging at the University Hospital Freiburg between January 2010 and December 2022 and for whom both the images and a report are available.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients who received radiological imaging at the University Hospital Freiburg between January 2010 and December 2022 and for whom both the images and a report are available.
Exclusion criteria:
Clinically usual modality-specific exclusion criteria; No Studies Specific Exclusion Criteria.
